cover.html: Welcome everyone. In this session we're going to trace the full arc of Observability — from its roots in network monitoring through to where we are today with AI-driven, proactive operations. Whether you're new to the space or looking to sharpen your pitch, by the end you'll have a clear mental model of why Observability matters and what separates the leaders from the laggards.
agenda.html: We've got six topics to cover. We'll start with the history — because understanding where we came from makes the current landscape make a lot more sense. Then we'll look at why modern architectures fundamentally broke the old monitoring model, dive into the core data signals, cover the standardisation story which is a huge tailwind right now, survey the competitive landscape, and finish with Elastic's specific differentiators.
history-monitoring.html: Let's start with history. In the 80s and 90s monitoring was essentially network monitoring — SNMP, ping checks, are-the-lights-green. By the 2000s we got application performance management and centralised log aggregation, but the model was still fundamentally reactive — users told you before your tools did. The 2010s is where things broke. Containers, Kubernetes, microservices — suddenly you had hundreds of ephemeral components instead of a few monoliths, and the old 'check if it's up' model simply didn't work anymore. The 2020s brought the response: distributed tracing, unified telemetry, and now AI-native platforms that can reason across all that data.
volume-problem.html: Here's the core problem in numbers. Modern applications generate 100 times more services to monitor than the monolith era. Studies consistently show 97 percent of alerts in enterprise environments are noise — which means alert fatigue is real and dangerous. And the average mean time to resolution for teams still relying on reactive monitoring is three and a half hours. The insight here is fundamental: you literally cannot hire enough engineers to watch dashboards at this scale. Observability is the application of machine reasoning to data volumes humans never could handle.
three-pillars.html: The three pillars are the foundation. Logs are your immutable event record — what happened, when, with all the context. They're the most human-readable signal but also the highest volume. Metrics are numeric measurements sampled over time — efficient, queryable, perfect for alerting and capacity planning. Traces are the newest of the three — they follow a single request across every service it touches, which is how you debug latency in a distributed system. The key takeaway: logs tell you what happened, metrics tell you how often, traces tell you why it was slow. You need all three to ask arbitrary questions about your system.
beyond-pillars.html: The three pillars get you most of the way, but modern platforms are expanding the signal set. Continuous profiling is the big emerging one — it tells you exactly which lines of code are burning your CPU or memory, turning 'slow' into an actionable code location. Real user monitoring captures actual user journeys and Core Web Vitals — backend health and user experience are not the same thing. Synthetics run scripted checks on your critical paths before real users hit problems. And infrastructure events — Kubernetes change events, deployment markers — give you the 'what changed' context that correlates with degradations.
standardization.html: Before standardisation every team instrumented differently. Correlating a database metric with an application trace with a Kubernetes log required custom ETL, brittle field mappings, and slow queries across siloed stores. OpenTelemetry — the CNCF standard — solved the collection layer. Instrument once with OTel SDKs and point the exporter wherever you want. No lock-in. Elastic Common Schema solves the storage layer — shared field names so cross-source search and ML work out of the box without a translation layer. And critically, consistent schema is the foundation that makes LLM-assisted root cause analysis actually work. This is a huge tailwind for the conversation right now.
competitive-landscape.html: Quick landscape survey. Datadog is the SaaS leader — strong integrations, polished UX, but high cost at scale and real data export friction. Dynatrace has the best enterprise AI story with the Davis engine and auto-discovery, but complex licensing. New Relic pivoted to consumption-based pricing and easy onboarding but the AI story is still maturing. Grafana with the LGTM stack is the open source champion — OTel-native and flexible, but there's operational overhead. Elastic's differentiated position is being the only platform that unifies observability, security, and search on a single data store — and that's increasingly where analysts are pointing customers as point-solution sprawl becomes the new technical debt.
elastic-differentiators.html: So why Elastic specifically? Four things. First, one store for everything — logs, metrics, traces, security events, business data, all in Elasticsearch. No cross-tool pivoting mid-incident. Second, search-first architecture — ad-hoc queries across petabytes in seconds. Most observability tools are BI tools dressed as monitoring. Elastic is a search engine first, which is a fundamentally different capability. Third, AI on your own data — the Elastic AI Assistant uses the LLM of your choice against your own indexed data. Your data doesn't leave your environment, and there's no vendor AI lock-in. Fourth, open by default — OTel-native ingestion, ECS schema, open source core. Elastic competes on value, not lock-in. That's a real differentiator when customers are burned from proprietary agents.
closing.html: Four things to take away. Monitoring evolved because architectures demanded it — reactive tools built for monoliths don't scale. The three pillars plus profiles, RUM, and synthetics give you full coverage. Standardisation with OTel and ECS pays compound dividends — it reduces cost today and unlocks AI tomorrow. And the industry is converging on unified platforms — point-solution sprawl is the new technical debt. The actionable next step is always the same: start with OpenTelemetry instrumentation. It's backend-agnostic today and opens every door, including Elastic's, when you're ready to consolidate. Any questions?
